# 5.1 Forwards and Futures

Forward contracts and their payoffs; the cost-of-carry model and no-arbitrage pricing; contango and backwardation; margin and mark-to-market in futures; hedging, the optimal hedge ratio and basis risk.

Key file: https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/ai/en/lessons/5.1-key.md

## Forward contracts

A bakery worries that wheat will be more expensive in six months, and a farmer worries that it will be cheaper. They can agree today that in six months the farmer will sell wheat to the bakery at 6 dollars a bushel. This is a **forward contract**: the two sides agree today to trade an asset at a future date $T$ at a price $F$ fixed today. The side that agrees to buy is long; the side that agrees to sell is short.

At maturity the long buys, at $F$, an asset whose market price is $S_T$, so the payoff is

$$
S_T - F
$$

The short's payoff is the opposite, $F - S_T$. A forward contract is a **derivative**: its value depends on the price of another asset (the underlying). Neither side pays anything at signing, so the contract's value is 0; afterwards, as the underlying price moves, one side's contract gains a positive value and the other's an equal negative value.

> (B) There is no loss at all, because nothing was paid at signing
> (C) It can choose not to perform and buy fuel at the market price
> (D) It makes money on the forward contract
>

## Cost-of-carry pricing

What should the forward price $F$ be? Consider an asset with price $S_0$ today that produces no income while held (a stock that pays no dividends, for example). There are two ways to own it at $T$: borrow today to buy it and hold it until $T$; or sign a forward contract and buy it then at $F$. Both give the same asset at $T$, so they must cost the same, or else there is arbitrage:

$$
F = S_0\,e^{rT}
$$

This uses continuous compounding (Lesson 0.1, "Compounding and the Time Value of Money" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/0-1-time-value-of-money/), with $r$ the risk-free rate. If the asset produces income while held, for example a stock index with dividend yield $q$, the holder of the spot asset receives that income, so the forward price must be correspondingly lower:

$$
F = S_0\,e^{(r - q)T}
$$

This is the **cost-of-carry model**: the forward price equals the spot price plus the net cost of holding the asset until maturity (the financing cost minus the income from the asset). If the market $F$ is above this price, arbitrageurs borrow to buy the spot asset and sell the forward (cash-and-carry); if it is below, they do the reverse. Covered interest parity in Lesson 2.7, "The Open Economy" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/2-7-open-economy/#interest-parity follows the same logic: the "income" of a foreign currency is the foreign interest rate.

For commodities, holding the physical good costs storage, but it also has a benefit: inventory can be used in production at any time and avoids running out; this benefit is called the convenience yield. Then $q$ is the convenience yield minus storage costs. A market in which forward prices are above the spot price is in **contango**; one in which they are below is in backwardation.

## Futures: margin and mark-to-market

Forward contracts are signed privately between two parties; one side may fail to perform at maturity, and they are hard to transfer before then. A **futures contract** standardizes the forward and trades it on an exchange: the quantity, the grade and the delivery date are fixed, and the exchange's clearinghouse becomes the seller to every buyer and the buyer to every seller.

To prevent default, futures require **margin**. An initial margin, usually only a few percent to a dozen or so percent of the contract's value, is deposited when the position is opened. Futures are settled every day at the closing price, which is called **mark-to-market**: when the price rises, the long's margin account grows and the short's shrinks; when an account falls below the maintenance margin, it must be topped up within a short time, or the position is closed out.

Margin gives futures high leverage: with margin of 10% of the contract value, a 1% price change moves the value of the margin by 10% (financial leverage). Mark-to-market also means losses must be paid in cash at once, even if the position will eventually make money (Exercises Question 2).

> **Check question C4**

> (B) Nothing happens, because the hedge offsets the gains and losses
> (C) The futures make money and the supply contracts lose money
> (D) The company can wait for oil prices to recover before topping up its margin
>

## Hedging and basis risk

**Hedging** uses derivatives to offset an existing risk: a farmer who will sell wheat sells futures (a short hedge), and an airline that will buy fuel buys futures (a long hedge). The purpose of hedging is not to raise the expected return but to reduce the uncertainty of the outcome: when prices rise, the futures gains offset the higher cost of the physical good, and when prices fall, the futures losses offset the savings.

Hedges are rarely perfect. The difference between the spot price and the futures price is called the **basis**. If the asset being hedged differs from the futures' underlying (jet fuel has no active futures market, for example, so heating-oil or crude futures are used instead), or the hedge date differs from the futures' delivery date, the basis changes and leaves some risk that cannot be removed, called basis risk.

How many futures are best then? The number of futures that minimizes the variance of the hedged position is the same quantity as the regression slope of Lesson 0.5, "Regression" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/0-5-regression/ and the beta of Lesson 4.4, "The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-4-capm/: the regression coefficient of spot price changes on futures price changes (Exercises Question 3). In the same way, index futures can adjust the beta of a stock portfolio: selling index futures reduces the portfolio's market risk without selling stocks (Lesson 4.5, "The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-5-single-index-model/#uses).

## Summary

- A forward contract fixes a price $F$ for a future trade; the long's payoff is $S_T - F$, and its value at signing is 0.
- The cost-of-carry model: $F = S_0e^{(r - q)T}$; deviations allow arbitrage. The forward price reflects the cost of carry; it is not a forecast of the future price.
- For commodities $q$ is the convenience yield minus storage costs; contango means $F > S$, backwardation $F < S$.
- Futures are standardized forwards: margin, mark-to-market, high leverage, and losses paid in cash at once.
- Hedging reduces uncertainty rather than raising expected returns; when the hedged asset differs from the futures' underlying there is basis risk; the optimal hedge ratio is the regression slope of spot on futures.

## Exercises

Assign them after the lesson. Answers and grading points are in the key file.

**Exercises Question 1 (id: Q1)**

A stock index is at 5,000, with a dividend yield of 1.5% a year (continuous) and a risk-free rate of 4% a year (continuous). The market price of the 1-year index futures is 5,180.
(a) By the cost-of-carry model, what should the futures price be? Is there an arbitrage opportunity? Describe the trade and its profit per index point at maturity.
(b) A financial commentator says: "The futures price is 3.6% above spot, which shows the market expects the index to rise 3.6% next year." Evaluate this statement.

**Exercises Question 2 (id: Q2)**

An investor buys 1 crude oil futures contract (1,000 barrels) at 80 dollars a barrel, with initial margin of 8,000 dollars and maintenance margin of 6,000 dollars; when margin falls short it must be restored to the initial level.
(a) The next day oil falls to 77 dollars. How much more margin must he post? On the 8,000 dollars he put in, what is that day's return?
(b) He says: "With only 8,000 dollars I control 80,000 dollars of oil, and the worst that can happen is losing these 8,000 dollars." If oil then falls to 70 dollars over the next few days, how much does he lose in total? Evaluate his statement.

**Exercises Question 3 (id: Q3)**

Jet fuel has no active futures market, so an airline hedges with heating-oil futures. In historical data, the monthly change in jet fuel prices has a standard deviation of 6%, the change in heating-oil futures prices 5%, and the correlation between them is 0.8.
(a) For each unit of jet fuel price exposure, with a position of $h$ units of futures against it, what is the variance of the combined price change? Find the $h$ that minimizes it. What is the standard deviation of the remaining monthly price change then?
(b) The airline's CFO says: "We have hedged at the optimal ratio, so our fuel price risk has been eliminated." Evaluate this statement. What determines the remaining risk?

**Exercises Question 4 (id: Q4)**

An oil fund holds front-month crude futures and, before each expiry, sells the front contract and buys the next month's (rolling). Suppose the spot price stays at 70 dollars a barrel all year and the futures curve keeps its shape: at each roll the front contract is sold at 70 dollars and the next month's bought at 70.7 dollars, and its price converges to the spot 70 at expiry.
(a) Ignoring interest on the margin, what is the fund's return over the year?
(b) An investor says: "I think oil will be at least 8% higher in a year, so I'll buy this oil fund and earn the rise in oil prices." Evaluate this statement.
